title: Norwegian media sue Meta over plans to use their journalism for AI
content:
Publishers say new terms for Facebook and Instagram business accounts could allow Meta to collect articles, images and videos from their websites without permission.
A coalition of Norwegian media organisations has launched legal action against Meta, arguing that the company’s new terms for business accounts could undermine publishers’ control over their own journalism and allow it to be used in AI products without their agreement.
According to the 10 media groups, the new terms would give Meta — which owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads — the right to collect their articles, photos and videos, including those behind a paywall, and use them to develop artificial intelligence products, among other things.
Meta quietly announced it was changing its Commercial Terms on 8 October, with plans to roll out on 30 October. However, the company postponed the roll-out after receiving widespread pushback from European publishers and antitrust authorities.
The launch is now set for 20 November, "to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what's changing and what's not", said Meta.
Critics say news publishers are being forced into an "all-or-nothing" choice by the US tech giant: allow Meta to scrape their journalism, potentially for AI training, or lose their Facebook and Instagram presence entirely.
The Norwegian media groups’ legal challenge will test whether publishers can block the changes before they take effect.
"The fear is that the companies will use this power to secure rights over journalistic content," the head of the Norwegian Media Businesses' Association (MBL), Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, said in a statement.
"Meta uses media groups' investments to develop artificial intelligence services that compete with them directly. This is both unacceptable and distorts competition," she added.
According to the plaintiffs, Meta’s new terms of use would apply to all professional account holders — media outlets as well as companies and retailers — and would leave them no way to opt out other than deleting their accounts.
They said they had filed a request with the Oslo District Court for a provisional injunction against the entry into force of the terms of use, pending a ruling on the substance of the case.
The plaintiffs include public broadcaster NRK, media groups Schibsted, Amedia, Polaris and Aller, as well as Norwegian news agency NTB.
On 14 October, MBL and NRK had also threatened to sue Meta, accusing the American tech giant of profiting from fraudulent advertisements impersonating them in order to defraud internet users.
A global shift
The Norwegian case reflects a broader dispute over the rights of publishers whose journalism appears on major tech and AI platforms.
Since May this year, more than 340 local and national news sites including the Guardian, the New York Times and USA Today have blocked internet archive crawler bots to prevent them from collecting data for training AI models.
And in June, France’s competition authority warned Meta that its approach to copyright talks with news outlets could "seriously harm" the press.

report.summary: Ten Norwegian media groups are seeking a court injunction to block Meta's new commercial terms, which they say would let Meta scrape their journalism—including paywalled content—for AI training without consent.
report.background: Meta quietly rewrote its Commercial Terms on 8 October, with an original effective date of 30 October, covering all professional accounts on Facebook and Instagram—media outlets, retailers and brands alike. After pushback from European publishers and antitrust regulators, Meta pushed the launch to 20 November. The dispute sits inside a much larger fight over who gets to convert journalism into AI training data. News organisations have watched crawler traffic, licensing negotiations and referral traffic all shift as generative AI products summarise content rather than link to it. Norway's case follows a French competition authority warning in June that Meta's copyright talks with publishers could 'seriously harm' the press, and a wave of news sites blocking archive crawlers. Because Norwegian press support and collective bargaining are strong, the country has become an early test case for whether publishers can stop terms-of-service changes before they take effect, rather than negotiating compensation afterwards.
key_points: The terms would let Meta harvest articles, images and videos from publisher sites—including content behind paywalls—and use them to build AI products. Publishers argue this converts years of editorial investment into free training material for a competitor, and that the only way to refuse is to delete their Facebook and Instagram accounts entirely.

Ten organisations are behind the challenge, including public broadcaster NRK, Schibsted, Amedia, Polaris, Aller and news agency NTB, coordinated by the Norwegian Media Businesses' Association (MBL). They have asked the Oslo District Court for a provisional injunction to freeze the terms until judges rule on the substance of the case.

Timing matters: Meta announced the change on 8 October, delayed the 30 October rollout after European pushback, and now plans 20 November, saying it needs time to 'explain what's changing and what's not.' The injunction request targets that window—a ruling before 20 November would be far more useful than one after.

The new terms apply to every professional account, not just newsrooms—retailers, brands and small businesses face the same all-or-nothing choice. That widens the potential coalition of objectors and raises the antitrust question MBL emphasises: Meta both distributes publishers' work and competes with them via AI.

Norway is one front in a global pushback. Since May, over 340 news sites including the Guardian, New York Times and USA Today have blocked archive crawlers; in June, France's competition authority warned Meta its copyright posture could 'seriously harm' the press. The tussle over fraudulent ads impersonating NRK adds to the tension.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the case tests whether platform terms of service can function as a de facto data-licensing regime, bypassing copyright negotiation entirely. A Norwegian injunction would encourage similar filings across Europe and strengthen the hand of collective-licensing bodies; a loss would confirm that publishers must accept scraping or exit major platforms. For developers, the immediate practical effect is more friction: expect tighter robots.txt enforcement, paywall-aware crawler blocking and licensing requirements for news-derived corpora, especially for models trained or deployed in the EU. For regular users, the likely outcome is less news availability on Facebook and Instagram, more AI-generated summaries replacing links to original reporting, and continued pressure on subscription-funded journalism as referral traffic erodes.
report.tools: To follow or act on this: Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control and AI Labyrinth (blocking and misdirecting AI crawlers), the emerging RSL (Really Simple Licensing) standard for machine-readable content licensing, Spawning's Do Not Train registry and HaveIBeenTrained search, C2PA Content Credentials for provenance, and Glaze/Nightshade for artists and photographers defending images. On the legal side, watch MBL's filings and the French competition authority's Meta case for precedent.
